entries.clue: Observe notch, we hear it's pretty to view (6)

indicatorNotes.we hear: What we hear is a noise rather than a spelling, so the words before it are wanted for their sound.

blocks.note: to observe something is to see it, and that noise opens the answer spelt this way
a notch cut in wood is a nick, and its sound finishes the answer spelt this way

annotation.surface: Someone points out a groove in the woodwork and adds that the spot is lovely to look at.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are wanted as sounds, not spellings: one word for observe and another for notch, and only run together do they spell anything at all. The comma between them counts for nothing once said aloud.
annotation.definitionFit: Scenic country is worth looking at for its own sake, which is what calling a place pretty to view says about it.

entries.clue: Retaliation offensive when playing Ludo, perhaps? (7-6)

blocks.note: Ludo is a children's board game played with small discs called counters
an offensive is a military attack

annotation.surface: The suggestion that hitting back is bad form in a game of Ludo.
annotation.walkthrough: Ludo is the British nursery board game in which each player moves four counters round a track, and 'perhaps' admits it is only one game that uses them. Offensive is the military noun, not the adjective the surface wants.
annotation.definitionFit: A counter-attack is the blow struck back at whoever attacked first, which is exactly what retaliation names.

entries.clue: After forty winks, family's getting serviettes (7)

indicatorNotes.After: After puts what comes next behind what has just been named, so the second piece follows the first.

blocks.note: forty winks is a short doze, a nap
kin is one's family, and the apostrophe-s hands over an S

annotation.surface: A household laying out the good linen once the after-dinner doze is over.
annotation.walkthrough: Forty winks is a short doze and kin is the old word for one's relatives. The apostrophe-s reads as 'is' in the sentence and hands over a letter instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Serviette is the everyday British word for the square of cloth or paper you wipe your hands on at table.

entries.clue: Money cleared, say, by airport desk (5-2)

indicatorNotes.say: Say asks for the noise a word makes rather than the spelling it is printed in.

blocks.note: a cheque is money on paper, and the sound of it is spelt this way in America
once a cheque has cleared the money is in, sitting in the account

annotation.surface: A payment that has gone through, dealt with at a counter in the airport.
annotation.walkthrough: Say asks for a sound. Money on paper is spelt one way in Britain and another in America, and the two are pronounced identically, so the noise settles which letters the grid gets.
annotation.definitionFit: The check-in is the desk where an airline takes your bags and hands over a boarding pass.

entries.clue: Short girl goes to country with one dog (6)

indicatorNotes.Short: Short asks for a clipped form, so the name beside it arrives cut down from its full length.

blocks.note: Sal is Sally cut down, the shortening the clue has just asked for
UK is the United Kingdom
i is the Roman numeral for one

annotation.surface: A little girl heading off to the countryside with a single dog in tow.
annotation.walkthrough: Country is the United Kingdom rather than the fields the surface paints, and the girl is named in full nowhere in the clue. Roman one supplies the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The saluki is a slender, silky-eared hound from the Middle East, one of the oldest breeds of dog there is.

entries.clue: By the way, beer is past its best (5)

blocks.note: a street is a way, and ST is its usual short form on a map
ale is beer

annotation.surface: An aside about beer that has been standing in the glass too long.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By the way' is the conversational idiom the surface leans on, and the way inside it is a street. Ale then follows directly, with nothing rearranged or hidden.
annotation.definitionFit: Beer or bread past its best has gone stale: flat, dry and no longer worth having.

entries.clue: Enjoys stories about king (5)

indicatorNotes.about: About means round, so the letters named before it close over the ones named after.

blocks.note: stories in the sense of fibs are lies
k is the short form chess and playing cards both use for the king

annotation.surface: Someone fond of the tales told about a monarch.
annotation.walkthrough: Stories are fibs here rather than tales, and the king arrives as the single letter that chess sets and playing cards both use for him.
annotation.definitionFit: To like something is to enjoy it, and both verbs take the same objects in the same third-person form.

entries.clue: Criticise about outcome of chain reaction (5-2,6)

blocks.note: to knock something is to criticise it
on means about, as in a book on birds
an effect is the outcome a cause produces

annotation.surface: Someone grumbling about where a chain reaction ended up.
annotation.walkthrough: To knock something is to criticise it, and on means about, as in a book on birds. 'Criticise about outcome' reads as one continuous grumble, which is how three separate pieces hide inside a single phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: One event setting off the next and the next is a chain reaction, which is the run of consequences a knock-on effect names.

entries.clue: Dodgy one, USA fuel company held writ (8)

indicatorNotes.Dodgy: Something dodgy is not what it appears to be, so its letters will not stay in the order printed.
indicatorNotes.held: What is held is kept inside, so the two letters named sit within the rest.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
BP, once British Petroleum, is the oil firm whose green-and-yellow sign stands over filling stations across Britain

annotation.surface: A shifty character and an American fuel firm on the wrong end of a court order.
annotation.walkthrough: Dodgy does the shuffling and held does the inserting, two instructions packed into one short sentence. The comma after 'one' is punctuation the setter may put wherever the surface needs it.
annotation.definitionFit: A subpoena is the writ ordering someone to appear in court or produce evidence, on pain of penalty.

entries.clue: Be aware of one thousand today (4)

blocks.note: k stands for a thousand, as in a salary quoted at 30k
today is the present time, now

annotation.surface: Being told to take account of a thousand of something before the day is out.
annotation.walkthrough: K for a thousand comes from kilo and turns up in salaries and race distances alike. Today and now are the same stretch of time in ordinary speech, which is what lets one stand for the other.
annotation.definitionFit: To know something is to be aware of it, the same act of holding a fact in mind.

entries.clue: Small case kept in perpetuity (4)

indicatorNotes.kept in: Something kept in a word is already sitting inside it, letter for letter.

blocks.note: the letters run unbroken through the middle of the word

annotation.surface: A little box put into storage for ever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kept in' is the instruction and perpetuity the hiding place, one long word doing all the concealing on its own. The surface promises for ever, which is what stops you looking at the letters themselves.
annotation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles, scissors and other little tools, carried in a pocket or hung at the waist.

entries.clue: It reminds you to stock Japanese wine (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a small sentence about what the thing does rather than a noun that could replace it, which is a standard way of cluing an object by its purpose.

blocks.note: a shop that stocks an item keeps it in
sake is the Japanese rice wine

annotation.surface: A note telling a shopkeeper to lay in some Japanese wine.
annotation.walkthrough: Sake is the Japanese rice wine, brewed from grain rather than pressed from fruit, and stock in the shopkeeper's sense is simply to keep. The definition says what the thing does instead of naming it.
annotation.definitionFit: A keepsake is kept precisely because it brings a person or an occasion back to mind every time you see it.

entries.clue: Where one might be found in the nick of time? (6)

annotation.definition: Where one might be found in the nick of time?

blocks.note: on the surface the idiom meaning with barely a moment to spare
read the other way, the nick is British slang for gaol and the time is the sentence served there

annotation.surface: Someone turning up with only a moment left before it was too late.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue rests on one idiom. Broken apart, the nick is British slang for a police station or gaol, and doing time is serving a sentence; nothing changes hands letter by letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A prison is where a convict is held, so it is where you would find someone who is in the nick and doing time.

entries.clue: Those out of this world, in sale, perhaps (6)

indicatorNotes.perhaps: Perhaps leaves the arrangement open, so the letters before it need not stay in the order printed.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: Goods in a sale being talked up as out of this world.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of this world' is shop language for a bargain on the surface and meant quite literally in the answer. 'Perhaps' is the only hint that the two words before it need rearranging.
annotation.definitionFit: Aliens come from somewhere other than Earth, so they are literally out of this world, the phrase the surface uses as praise.

entries.clue: Prisoner's account, note, is second-hand (7)

blocks.note: ac is the short form of account on a bank statement
c is a musical note, the one a scale of C starts on
a second-hand car is a used one

annotation.surface: A convict's version of events turning out to be borrowed from somebody else.
annotation.walkthrough: Account shortens the way it does on a bank statement, and the note is the musical kind rather than a memo or a banknote. Second-hand is a plain synonym doing the work at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: The figure standing trial in the dock is called the accused, and British courts long referred to that same person as the prisoner at the bar.

entries.clue: Sick bird sounds unlawful (7)

indicatorNotes.sounds: Sounds asks for the noise a word makes rather than the letters it is written with.

blocks.note: someone sick is ill
the bird is an eagle, and saying it aloud after the first piece finishes the word this way

annotation.surface: The noise an ailing bird makes, apparently against the law.
annotation.walkthrough: Sounds reads as the noise a poorly bird makes and is really the instruction to say a word rather than spell it. Only the second half is sounded; the first is taken exactly as it stands.
annotation.definitionFit: Something illegal is forbidden by law, which is what unlawful says about it.

entries.clue: Holding breath let icon physically fit (8)

indicatorNotes.Holding: What a phrase is holding lies inside it, so the letters are read straight off in order.

blocks.note: the letters run unbroken across the three words, starting partway through the first

annotation.surface: A held breath and an icon allowed through.
annotation.walkthrough: Holding is the instruction to look inside, and the letters cross three words without a break. Long hidden answers keep best in a phrase that means almost nothing, which is what this surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: An athletic person is in the trained, muscular shape that being physically fit describes.

entries.clue: In practice, he deputises (5)

blocks.note: on the surface the phrase meaning in reality, as against in theory
read the other way, the practice is a doctor's or solicitor's and he is the stand-in hired to run it

annotation.surface: A claim that in reality the man stands in for other people.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In practice' reads as the phrase that sets reality against theory. The other reading makes it a doctor's or solicitor's practice, the place a temporary stand-in is paid to cover while the regular is away.
annotation.definitionFit: A locum is the doctor, dentist or solicitor engaged to fill someone's place in their practice for a spell.

entries.clue: Now find party up in the river (5)

indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry up runs against the writing, so the letters come back the way they went.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts one set of letters inside the other rather than beside it.

blocks.note: the Tay is Scotland's longest river, running through Perth to the North Sea
a party is a do, turned round as the clue asks

annotation.surface: A celebration being tracked down somewhere up the river.
annotation.walkthrough: A do is a party, one of the shortest words in the setter's kit. Up in a down entry sends it back the way it came, and the river closes over it.
annotation.definitionFit: Today is the day that is now, and the two swap freely in ordinary speech about when something happens.

entries.clue: Existence of some mortal if existing (4)

indicatorNotes.of some: Of some asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it.

blocks.note: the letters straddle the three words, one from the first, all of the second and one from the third

annotation.surface: Wondering whether a particular mortal is still around.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of some' asks for a part of what follows rather than all of it. Short hidden answers can start at the very end of a word, which is where this one begins.
annotation.definitionFit: Life is the state of being alive, which is existence in the plainest sense of the word.

entries.clue: Powder found in hospital cabinets (4)

indicatorNotes.found in: What is found in a phrase is already sitting there in its letters, waiting to be read off.

blocks.note: the letters bridge the join between the two words

annotation.surface: Dusting powder turning up in the cupboards of a hospital ward.
annotation.walkthrough: Powder sitting in hospital cabinets is exactly where you would expect to find it, so the surface gives nothing away by being perfectly true. The letters bridge the gap between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Talc is the soft mineral ground down to make talcum powder, the white dust sold for dusting skin.

entries.clue: Intended to insert notice in the document (8)

indicatorNotes.insert: To insert a thing is to push it into something else, so one set of letters goes within the other.
indicatorNotes.in: In names the place the inserted letters end up, inside what follows rather than beside it.

blocks.note: a deed is a legal document, such as the deeds to a house
a sign is a notice put up for people to read

annotation.surface: Slipping an announcement into an official paper.
annotation.walkthrough: A deed is the legal document that proves who owns a house, and a sign is a notice. 'Insert ... in' spells the containment out rather than dressing it up as something else.
annotation.definitionFit: Something designed to happen was intended to happen; both words say it was meant rather than accidental.

entries.clue: Revealing sleeper embracing girl (6)

indicatorNotes.embracing: To embrace is to put your arms right round something, so the letters close over what is named next.

blocks.note: a sleeper is an agent planted years ahead and left dormant until wanted, which is to say a spy
Kim is a girl's name

annotation.surface: Someone asleep with their arms round a girl, and the scene giving something away.
annotation.walkthrough: A sleeper is a spy planted long in advance and left inactive until called on, not somebody having a nap. Kim serves as the girl, one of the short names setters keep permanently on hand.
annotation.definitionFit: Skimpy clothing barely covers, so it reveals; revealing is the everyday word for that same short measure of cloth.

entries.clue: Take out permit entering river (6)

indicatorNotes.entering: What is entering something passes inside it, so these letters land within the ones named next.

blocks.note: the Dee is a river twice over, one flowing through Chester and another through Aberdeen
to let someone do something is to permit it

annotation.surface: Buying the licence you need before wading into the river.
annotation.walkthrough: The Dee is a river twice over, one in Wales and the north-west, another in Scotland, and setters use it for either. Permit is the verb here, not the licence the surface hands you.
annotation.definitionFit: To delete a word is to take it out of the text, striking it from what stands on the page.
